People who sold the farm for non-1.01 2027 picks are going to be disappointed.

Jeremiah Smith is truly generational – that’s leave that aside.

Jadan Baugh is also great (3-year producer; career .293 MTF/attempt) – but certainly not a Bijan or even Ashton Jeanty-level prospect. 

Baugh currently projects as a late-RD1/early-RD2 NFL Draft pick & there are aspects of his profile which people will nitpick: 3-Star Recruit; career 3.47 YAC/attempt isn’t special; the receiving has been non-existent in 2/3 seasons (5 receptions as a freshman, just 3 this season; although he had 33 receptions on 40 targets as a sophomore). Think Breece Hall/Kenneth Walker in terms of prospect strength. 

Beyond that?

The “consensus” WR2 coming into the year (Cam Coleman) has not had a game with more than 4 receptions or 70 yards this year; his career 1.74 YPRR would rank dead-last amongst all RD1 WR prospects since 2020 – even worse than Xavier Legette (1.75 career YPRR). 

Coleman has a very mediocre target-earning profile (career .185 TPRR), high contested-target-rate (24.2%), isn’t a YAC-threat (career 2.6 YAC/reception; career .152 MTF/reception), etc, etc.

Charlie Becker looks better (career 3.65 YPRR; more than double Coleman’s) – & is a projected Top-5 overall pick in Nate Tice’s latest mock draft for Yahoo (released yesterday).

Mick Marsh (projected 31st overall) is the only other WR Tice has mocked inside the 1st round. Eric Edholm (also of Yahoo) has Ryan Coleman-Williams projected 23rd. There are no other projected RD1 WR’s.

Arch Manning will get drafted highly (Top-5 in both mocks) & will be a coveted dynasty trade chip due to his name power – but certainly has far from a flawless profile (below 8.0 Y/A each of the last 2 seasons).

The main QB risers (Mestemaker & Austin Simmons) could still go back to school.

There will be QB’s drafted in the first 2 rounds of the NFL Draft – but those QB’s could be late-RD1/early-RD2 picks & may get the redshirt treatment as rookies (Ty Simpson comes to mind as a comparable example).

Tice’s 1st round mock has them projected:

- Mestemaker (5th)
- Simmons (9th)
- Chambliss (21st)

No other QB’s included.

Eric Edholm’s (also of Yahoo) 1st round mock has them projected:

- Chambliss (6th)
- Mestemaker (9th)
- Mensah (13th)
- Moore (21st)

There’s also time for these QB’s to fall out of the RD1 discussion completely – or return back to school (in Mestemaker’s, Mensah’s, & Simmons’ case).

The TE Class is strong & could have 3-4 TE’s drafted in the first 2 rounds.

But the two TE’s projected to get RD1 NFL Draft capital do not have strong target-earning profiles.

- Jamari Johnson (career .180 TPRR)
- Trey’Dez Green (career .192 TPRR)

TJ Hockenson, OJ Howard, & Hayden Hurst are the only RD1 TE’s in the past decade with worse collegiate target-earning profiles.

People who sold their souls for 2027 picks are going to be shocked when it comes time to actually make them.

Through four games, the Eagles’ rush defense ranks 28th in success rate, 23rd in EPA, and 24th in stuff percentage. With a likely favorable game script, Tuten is positioned to perform well. Additionally, on the season he’s averaging a ridiculous 0.22 missed tackles forced per attempt.

I like Jaylen to bounce back in a major way this week.

15. The Commanders are going to be without Stefon Diggs this week, and Terry McLaurin is a true game-time decision, which sets up Antonio Williams to have himself a day against a Giants secondary that ranks middle of the pack in EPA and success rate. Dennard Wilson’s defense has also primarily run Cover 1/3/4 from a coverage perspective this season. Versus those coverages this season, Antonio Williams is averaging 1.96 YPRR with a 0.28 TPRR. With Jayden Daniels returning from injury, Williams is set to be the Commanders’ leading receiver in this matchup.

NFL Week 5 Preview

Here’s what I’m looking at on this slate

- Bears icon Mike Ditka passed away on Friday, adding yet another layer to this week’s already intriguing installment of Bears at Packers.

- The pressure is on Green Bay in this spot. They are reeling, they are down their two best defensive players, they have the worst offensive line they’ve had in recent memory, but they also have their starting quarterback in Jordan Love and despite their struggles, they are still a manageable 2-2.

- From Green Bay’s end, I would expect them to have a game plan more tailored to their current reality coming off a long week. Speedster duo Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are the team’s biggest matchup problem for opponents, but the Packers have been very pass heavy and it’s nearly impossible to effectively throw downfield without reliable pass protection. Even more so when you have no run game and opposing pass rushers can pin their ears back. So, I’m expecting Green Bay to try to get their running game going more here, while leaning into more manufactured touches and quicker route combinations in the passing game. If they have success in this sense, then I’d expect a few downfield shots to their speedsters.

- On the Bears end, I’d make Green Bay show they can consistently stop the run given Chicago’s current situation. Kyle Monangai is out with turf toe, so there should be a lot on D’Andre Swift’s plate with Roschon Johnson supplementing.

- I would not put this game in Tyson Bagent’s hands unless I absolutely have to, he was a few plays and a couple penalties away from having a nightmare game against the Jets last week.

- Speaking of, a second wrinkle in this game is Caleb Williams had a limited practice Friday and was listed as questionable as of Friday night. I would guess that was a test run for Week 6, perhaps Week 7, but interesting, nevertheless, especially given the opponent and the important of Ditka to the city of Chicago. I’d get it if Caleb was pushing to play, but I hope he isn’t rushed back.

- Seahawks vs. 49ers is the best matchup on Sunday.

- San Francisco has one of the better coaches in Kyle Shanahan and Brock Purdy has been better than most realize for several years. That said, I think public perception is flying a little high on the Niners, and a trip to Seattle is a tremendous test for Purdy and this offense, who were shut down until the 4thquarter against Denver last week.

- Seattle gave up 26 points to the 49ers over three games last season, including just 9 across their Week 18 tilt and Division Round matchup, both Seahawks victories.

- I mentioned this once recently; Bill Belichick would treat Jaxon Smith-Njigba like a punt gunner on gotta have it passing situations. He would not like JSN beat him in those spots and quite frankly, I’m not sure why no one is trying this. Fear of being different and wrong, I’d expect.

- From what I have seen, Sam Darnold is still a solid quarterback but Seattle’s offense is a step less without Klint Kubiak, and perhaps Kenneth Walker. If the 49ers win this game, I’d expect their defense to drive that outcome, like they did against Denver last week.

- The Jaguars vs. Eagles game in London has seen an enormous line movement from -2.5 to -7.5. I do not recall a line movement that large that wasn’t related to a quarterback injury. Given that, it would be Jaguars or pass for me, as the Eagles have so many injuries, a greatly reduced offensive line, and I have no hope that their offensive coaching staff will create any margin against what has been a very good Jaguars defense with a top 10 front.

- In truth, this looks like a potential implosion spot for Philadelphia’s offense, against a Jaguars team that is looking like a contender.

- If the Eagles have a shot in this game, their defense needs to play up and carry them. In particular, their underachieving front four needs to play their best game of the year against a middling Jaguars offensive line. Edge Jonathan Greenard, who has been banged up, could really give the Eagles’ a boost if he’s near full strength.

- The problem with that is Trevor Lawrence has become who everyone has thought he was going to be under Liam Coen.

- I sincerely hope Jayden Daniels is completely fine and not risking his future playing in this game. Given that, really high chance Washington goes out of their way to protect Daniels, which looks like run centric game plan, quick hitter passing game, Daniels only runs if he has a clear lane.

- One interesting aspect the Giants have going forward against Washington is New York has a very rangy linebacker group that should help them manage mobile quarterbacks like Daniels.

- If I’m Washington, I run at very talented, but 252 lbs edge Abdul Carter to both try and neutralize him on pass sets and because he can be moved in the run game.

- From what I’ve seen, the Giants should give Tyrone Tracy some significant run starting this week. Najee Harris is a professional running back, but he has limited juice and he fumbled last week. Cam Skattebo, as physical and as hard of a runner as there is, looks like his burst is already down. Mixing Tracy with Skattebo would give opposing defenses much different looks.

- Jameis Winston is a wild card. He’s a backup that is capable of throwing for 300 yards without it being an accident, but he’s also capable of losing a game entirely on his own. He had good games against the Lions and Packers last year, but he has not been very good in Jaxson Dart’s absence this season, though he did at least have some positive moments last week against Arizona.

- I am not a Tyler Shough guy, but I was open to being wrong after how well he played in Baltimore in Week 2. Despite that moment of doubt, I don’t think I’m wrong. Shough facing Brian Flores’ defense, while being without his left tackle, is a very messy situation. I’m very curious to see what Kellen Moore tries to do against Flores. Given that Moore was a college QB and he’s coming off a real rocky game in Atlanta, I’m expecting an uptick in screens and quick hitters.

- Minnesota is down the left side of their offensive line. While the Saints don’t have a high-end front to really take advantage of that, it’s still a huge limitation for Kyler Murray, who was fine against bottom of the barrel Miami but he’s been mediocre as a Viking so far.

- Starting today I’m going to begin openly wondering aloud if Brian Daboll is among the worst active play callers in the NFL. I thought he was bad in New York, he’s shown me nothing in Tennessee.

- The Texans pass rush has an advantage in this game, and they are coming off one of, if not their worst showing in years against Dallas last week, in an absolute must win game at 0-4.

- I have no confidence in Daboll and I’d be pretty surprised if Houston’s defense doesn’t bounce back in a significant way, but the Titans path to an upset is their own front taking over this game. CJ Stroud has played pretty well this season, but the Texans have a sub part offensive line and the one true strength of the Titans football program is their front, headlined by interior disruptor Jeffery Simmons.

- Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are currently both still questionable, but truth be told I think Joe Burrow’s Bengals can still win this game even if both play makers miss. First, I don’t think Burrow needs his elite play makers to have an efficient game on offense, against this bottom tier pass rush/ secondary combo.

- Cincinnati’s front four is also going to be a problem for Miami’s offensive line.

- I think the Jets beat the Browns in a game between two teams that are pretty similar roster wise. If anything, the Jets offensive line is ahead of Cleveland’s, where I’d say New York is a better landing spot for a new future at quarterback.

- The X factor here is Deshaun Watson, who is still not Houston level Watson, but he’s currently enjoying his best run since joining Cleveland. Todd Monken and the Brown’s young, talented skill group deserve a good amount of the credit for that, but I first noted that Watson played promisingly in Week 2 and that has been a thing for three games in a row.

- KC Concepcion could be a problem if Cleveland can get him in space against the Jets.

- Geno Smith is the poster child for the idea that sacks are a quarterback stat, because he takes some of the worst sacks you’ll ever seen. Mason Graham being out is one of the reasons I lean Jets, because New York can provide help on Jared Verse without much reservation.

- I’d put Klint Kubiak in the Dave Canales and Liam Coen cluster for coaches, which is a compliment. That also makes Kubiak vs. Mike Vrabel a really interesting coaching matchup.

- Kirk Cousins has played very well so far and Kubiak has elevated this offense. Specifically, I absolutely love how he’s leaning into Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer as the core of the passing offense (along with Ashton Jeanty). Good coaches use what they have instead of trying to fit square pegs into round holes. I’m really looking forward to seeing how Vrabel tries to handle Bowers.

- I’d cluster the Raiders pass rush with Buffalo’s, more of a mid-range pass rush (Buffalo’s is better but has a worse headliner), so I expect Drake Maye to be fine in this matchup.

- The Steelers are coming off a long week and a loss, to face a Colts team coming off a London game. Given Pittsburgh’s second half schedule, this is close to a must win.

- I imagine that Shane Steichen isn’t going to come out slinging it with Daniel Jones against this defense, especially not after last week where Jones was atrocious on foreign soil. I would think muddy, run centric game plan, try to keep this game close and ugly for as long as possible is the Colts best path. If the Colts’ defense fails them against a flawed Steelers offense, Indianapolis could be in trouble here.

- Monster tight end Darnell Washington saw some interesting usage against Cleveland last week. To Mike McCarthy’s credit, which is a phrase that was not easy for me to say, it seems like he and his staff have recognized that Washington is a pretty unique player in the league and maybe they should do more with him. Kudos to them, I hope to see it continue.

- The Chargers offensive line was already bad in the interior, now they are down both of their offensive tackles, who are two of the four best players on the whole team. This Chargers offensive line this week is among the worst I’ve ever seen assembled, and they are facing a quality Broncos front.

- If there is one positive for the Chargers offense, it’s that both of Denver’s perimeter corners are out.

- Sean Payton is taking over play calling duties, so I’d expect this game to go through the run game behind this offensive line, with Jaylen Waddle seeing a spike in usage, including some manufactured touches.

- On a personal level, I’ve always thought Sean Payton was a very good play caller that sets things up and leans into what his team has personnel wise. I saw nothing over the last four weeks that made me think Davis Webb should be running the offense instead of Payton.

- The Cardinals are down their left tackle and Jacoby Brissett was bad in New York last week, and I mean bad. If that version Brissett is close to what we see on Sunday, behind what is now a significantly less reliable offensive line with Paris Johnson out against a top 10ish Lions pass rush, I could see Detroit winning this game with some distance.

- If Brissett plays well, which we’ve seen at times in Arizona over the last 12 months, this game will shoot out as expected.

- If Marvin Harrison Jr. still doesn’t do much against this Lions’ injury depleted secondary, it’s at least time for a change of scenery.

- The truth of the Atlanta Falcons is somewhere in the middle of their first two, brutal games without Michael Penix, and their last two blowout victories with Penix. They get lucky in drawing the Ravens with Lamar Jackson sidelined, which has become a pretty frequent occurrence for Baltimore.

- Tyler Huntley isn’t a bad backup quarterback. I envision the Ravens trying to ride Derrick Henry with Zay Flowers seeing pretty concentrated volume.

- No Trey Hendrickson is a pretty big blow to Baltimore, as they’ll likely need to bring heat to pressure Penix.

- I could envision the Ravens containing Bijan Robinson, same with Drake London, as Jessie Minter was able to keep both players in relative check with a worse defensive roster the last time he faced Atlanta (although Kirk Cousins was the Falcons QB in that matchup).

- It would not shock me if Baltimore forced a few turnover Sunday night.

- Rams vs. Bills is among the best possible matchups the NFL has to offer in 2026. LA has a better roster than Buffalo, even with Myles Garrett sidelined. They also have the better coach, making this a bit of a Josh Allen vs. the world kind of matchup.

- Both teams are top 10 in both trenches.

- Puka Nacua and Davante Adams against the Bills secondary looks like a pretty significant advantage for the Rams. I’d imagine Puka in particular is a very unique cover for cornerbacks that haven’t faced him. Not just because of his physicality, but because of when Matthew Stafford will give him targets (as soon as he breaks, when he’s covered, throws to spots). It’s a pretty unique dynamic to deal with.

- The last time Nacua faced Buffalo he went 12-162-1.

I have watched every NFL game for roughly a decade. I have done this for the purpose of sports speculation.

I run a reality-based program here.

Engagement is how I reach new users. So as long as engagement remains strong (comments/ shares) I’ll continue pumping this and similarly detailed insights out every week.

NFL Team Notes: NFC East (Quarter Pole)

Dallas Cowboys (2-3)

- Coming off a bad loss where everything that could have gone wrong, did, on Thursday Night Football, the long-term reality for the Cowboys is they are a middle-of-the-pack team with a good offense and a liability of a defense.

- Dak Prescott is what he is, he’s good, but he’s never been an upper echelon guy like your Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, etc. Prescott is in the tier below those guys, the very good, but not quite great.

- Years ago I had something called the Dak to Carr spectrum, to basically illustrate the range of quarterbacks that have the capacity to go beat Mahomes or Allen in a regular season game, but not with any consistency. Dak was at the top of that group, Derek Carr at the back. That range is league average starter, which starts around 10th and ends around 20th. That’s what Dak is, front end of league average starter.

- A few years ago Dak had an all star team around him and Dallas was a very real threat during that span, but that’s been over for several years now. That was the peak for Prescott’s Cowboys, where now he and the wide receiver duo of CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens form the only true core strength of this team.

- Defensively, the Cowboys have some quality players but as a group they have been a disaster to this point with no obvious strength to hang their hat on defensively. Not much of a pass rush, pretty bad tackling in space with a secondary that should be better than they are.

- Kicker Brandon Aubrey is a unique asset in the sense that if the Cowboys are down by 3 late, if they can get to the 50-yard line they have a very good chance to go to overtime. No one else quite has that, so it warrants mentioning.

- Perhaps my biggest concern with Dallas is not only was the hiring of Brian Schottenheimer a full throttled head scratcher, but the worst aspect of their loss on Thursday night is Dallas was outcoached by Todd Bowles’ Buccaneers. That’s not good.

- A close to ceiling outcome for the 2026 Cowboys would be to win the NFC East and lose in the Wild Card round to one of the teams in the NFC West. Maybe Dallas hosts Detroit in the Wild Card, beats them in a close game between two similar teams, and then loses in the Division Round.

New York Giants (3-1)

- The foundation of this team’s future is blue chip defensive talents Abdul Carter and Arvel Reese.

- I’m not sure what the Giants do with Reese long term, meaning does he continue to play off ball linebacker while seeing some edge reps like Micah Parsons did early in his career, or, like Parsons, will Reese one day be a full-time edge. Reese still has room for improvement in coverage, but he’s already a very obvious difference maker.

- It looks like Carter gets routinely game planned for, as he sees a lot of double teams on obvious passing downs, which isn’t a surprise for me. New York’s pass rush has been mostly underwhelming this season considering that they have four former first round edge talents, but Carter showed high-end talent late last season and it’s very obvious he’s a premium athlete at the position. I have said a few times that Carter is on the Will Anderson career track.

- Part of me hopes the Giants future defense has Carter and Reese as full-time edge players.

- Brian Burns being out for the year is a pretty significant blow to New York’s very talented, but underperforming edge group.

- I’m very curious to see how the combination of Reese and veteran Tremaine Edmunds helps New York with mobile quarterbacks, as that is a very rangy linebacker duo.

- New York’s secondary is notably better this year, with safety Jevon Holland taking a noticeable step in the right direction under the new staff. Deonte Banks and George Newsome are former first round picks with a lot at stake this season and I love giving guys like that opportunities. It’s good business, and so far it’s worked out pretty well.

- Some people like Jameis Winston, but he’s hard for me to watch. Last week against Arizona was the perfect Winston game, as he mixed some genuinely high-end throws with at least one truly bad decision and a late game layup to extend a drive that he missed by a preposterous amount. When Winston’s on, he can keep you in a game against an elite offense, but he can hand an opponent a win on a silver platter just as well.

- If you’re a Giants fan you’re not going to like this, I did not care at all about Jaxson Dart’s performance against Dallas on opening night because, as we saw Thursday against the Bucs, the Cowboys are a bad defense and a very beatable team. We’ll see how Dart looks next year but don’t overcount that win, as it was a home win against a middle-of-the-road team with no pass rush and holes everywhere on their defense.

- The interesting aspect of J.J. McCarthy is he has the same relative skillset as Dart, McCarthy is just less interesting.

- It would make sense if Tyrone Tracy was given some opportunities over the coming weeks, as this run game could use some juice.

- Cam Skattebo is an animal, a one of a kind in terms of hard running. His long-term future would be best served as a closer. Him seeing a ton of work to close out games the Giants are winning, with fresh legs against near the end defenses would be fascinating.

- Skattebo being a featured back is going to be hard to sustain, as him taking 20 carries is really more like 50 with the physical, contact seeking way he runs, and he’s been gradually showing a reduction in burst/ speed over the last few weeks, especially last week.

- Malik Nabers looked the closest he’s looked to being himself last week. Isaiah Likely is a better fit for Dart than Winston, but he’s still a solid second option in this passing game. Malachi Fields looks like a nice contested catch role player long term.

- So far, the Giants are well ran under John Harbaugh, while Matt Nagy doesn’t provide much strategic margin on offense and the defense has both been improved on the backend while the pass rush has underwhelmed outside of the second half against Arizona last week, who aren’t exactly marching out a premium offensive line.

- This division is bad enough where the Giants aren’t drawing dead at winning it given their schedule, but their lives would be made much easier if they win the next two against the Commanders and Saints.

Philadelphia Eagles (2-2)

- Premium offensive line play has been a hallmark of the Eagles throughout this century. Between Landon Dickerson landing on IR and Lane Johnson retiring, this is the worst offensive line Philadelphia has had that I can remember. Cam Jurgens being traded in season also warrants mention, even though he’s underwhelmed recently.

- The Eagles front four, another strength of the team for the past 20+ years, has been down as well. Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis remain a formidable interior duo, even though you could argue that they are better in theory than in actuality. I say that as someone that thought they’d be wrecking games regularly the moment Carter was drafted. Regardless, once edge Jonathan Greenard gets back to full strength, there is at least a path to the Eagles’ front four being a top 10 unit like they should be.

- The Eagles injury report right now has 10 current starters listed as questionable. Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith both have hamstring injuries while Dallas Goedert has missed the last two games.

- The Eagles’ uncharacteristically struggling offensive line and them being without their three best skill players can certainly explain some of Jalen Hurts struggles, but not all of them.

- The Eagles also have no strategic advantage on offense currently. When I watch them it strikes me as if they are just calling plays, which is a phrase I’ve used for years when describing play callers I see very little from. So the deck is genuinely stacked against Hurts.

- However, for each of the last two years when I watch the Eagles’ offense, it’s usually a variant of the same, kind of hard to watch underperformance given the talent they have on this roster. Hurt has played two of the best games of his career in Super Bowls, so the ceiling is massive, but week-to-week, I could name 15 guys off the top of my head that I’d rather have at the position over the past two seasons.

- Nick Sirianni is a very fortunate man that he was given this opportunity with the Eagles, who have the league’s best front office. I’d give Sirianni very little credit for their success and it seems rather obvious that the team should be looking for a new coach next offseason.

- The loss to the Bears was bad, last week’s loss to the Rams struck me as a backbreaker, just an absolutely brutal loss.

- The only reason the Eagles still have a shot to win the NFC East is lack of high-end competition.

Washington Commanders (1-3)

- I hope Jayden Daniels elbow is fine, because if he’s rushing back they are out of their minds risking him long term.

- Before his injury against Dallas, Daniels looked like he was going to put up 400+ yards of offense, probably with over 100 on the ground. He is the one thing that makes Washington interesting.

- Marcus Mariota played very well against Seattle, but I also thought Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough had a really good game plan and that he did a fantastic job of mitigating Seattle’s pass rush. Other teams should borrow from his game plan for the Seahawks.

- I also thought the Commanders’ offensive line played a very strong game in that contest, given their talent level.

- Washington probably has the worst running back room in the league, despite being a team that should stylistically lean into having a premium player at the position, for the same reason pairing Derrick Henry with Lamar Jackson is a unique problem for opposing defenses to solve.

- The Commanders group of pass catchers are fine when everyone is healthy, but I wouldn’t exactly call them a strength, either.

- Washington is well coached defensively, but they lack difference making talent.

- Their front is on the back side of average and their secondary is a bottom third type group.

- LB Sonny Styles was drafted to be an elite linebacker, and he’s already shown that promise in coverage. He’s had his two best games over the past two weeks.

- Ultimately Washington has the worst non-quarterback roster in the division, but they also have the second-best coach and I’d personally take Daniels over Dak Prescott.

I will do the NFC West next Tuesday morning, I may do more, I may not, we’ll see.

THIS WEEK IN EL SALVADOR

Vol. 16 | October 4–10, 2026

Presidential approval, landmark gang convictions, economic growth, foreign investment, tourism, infrastructure and artificial intelligence.

El Salvador entered October with a series of developments spanning public opinion, justice, international investment, tourism, infrastructure and technology.

President Nayib Bukele topped a new international approval ranking. Two convicted MS-13 gang members received life sentences. The World Bank raised its economic growth forecast, Chevron announced plans for another major investment, and the country's principal international airport surpassed four million passengers.

Meanwhile, construction continued on a 50,000-seat national stadium, Honduran visitors arrived for Semana Morazánica, and Salvadoran institutions presented new tools to support investment and urban planning.

Together, these developments offer a broad picture of the issues shaping El Salvador's final quarter of 2026.

1. 🇸🇻 BUKELE LEADS INTERNATIONAL APPROVAL RANKING WITH 90%

President Nayib Bukele opened the week at the top of Mitofsky's latest international ranking of presidential approval.

According to the September 2026 results published by Mitofsky and TResearch, Bukele registered 90% approval, placing first among 40 national leaders evaluated worldwide.

The Salvadoran president responded to the results on X with a short message: “La cima es solitaria…” — “It's lonely at the top.”

The ranking represents another notable international public-opinion result for a president whose administration has placed security, infrastructure, investment and economic development at the center of its agenda.

2. ⚖️ HISTORIC LIFE SENTENCES FOR TWO MS-13 GANG MEMBERS
El Salvador's justice system delivered one of the week's most significant security developments on October 9.

The Fourth Organized Crime Court of San Salvador sentenced two members of MS-13 to life imprisonment.

The convicted men were identified as Josué Germain González Mejía, described by prosecutors as a corredor de clica, or clique-level leader, and Giovanni Andrés Hernández, identified as a homeboy, a recognized gang member.

According to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), prosecutors established that the defendants exercised criminal control over areas of San Salvador and surrounding communities. The prosecution linked their activities to homicides, disappearances, extortion and other organized-crime offenses.

Both men had been arrested under the state of exception introduced in March 2022 and subsequently prosecuted.

These are among the first life sentences imposed on MS-13 members under El Salvador's new sentencing framework, representing a notable development in the prosecution of organized crime. They were not, however, the country's first life sentences overall.

The development comes alongside other convictions. On October 8, the FGR reported that 52 members of the Soya Criminal Locos Salvatruchos clique, including six leaders, received sentences ranging from 20 to 48 years for crimes including illicit association, drug offenses, injuries and aggravated robbery.

Prosecutors said the group had operated in several Soyapango communities, including El Limón, Villa Kiwanis, Los Arenales, Santa Rosa and Guayacán.

These rulings illustrate how the country's security strategy continues to extend from arrests and territorial enforcement into the courtroom, with prosecutors seeking long-term sentences against convicted gang members.

3. 📈 WORLD BANK RAISES EL SALVADOR’S 2026 GROWTH FORECAST TO 4.5%

El Salvador received another important economic development this week as the World Bank raised its growth outlook for 2026 to 4.5%.

The updated forecast places El Salvador among the stronger-performing economies in Latin America this year and, according to the reporting released October 6, ahead of its Central American neighbors in projected economic expansion.

The World Bank identifies improving security conditions, stronger private investment, construction activity and consumption as important factors supporting the economy.

The institution also recognizes the importance of fiscal consolidation and continued reforms in strengthening economic stability and investor confidence.

The new projection follows an extended period of improving economic activity, including the expansion of construction, tourism and private investment.

President Bukele highlighted the revised forecast on X, drawing attention to the country's improved economic outlook.

For perspective, the World Bank reports that El Salvador's economy expanded by 3.9% in 2025, following 2.6% growth in 2024.

4. 💰 CHEVRON ANNOUNCES NEARLY $90 MILLION IN NEW INVESTMENT
International energy company Chevron announced plans to invest approximately $90 million in El Salvador.

According to the October 9 announcement, the investment will focus on expanding fuel-storage capacity and opening additional service stations in areas experiencing commercial and urban development.

The new commitment follows approximately $55 million invested by the company since 2020.

The expansion is relevant not only to the energy sector but also to transportation, logistics, commerce and the broader infrastructure supporting economic activity.

As new residential, industrial and commercial developments emerge, the country's fuel-distribution network must also adapt to changing demand.

Chevron's announcement adds another major corporate investment plan to El Salvador's growing pipeline of private-sector projects.

5. 🇺🇸 US INVESTMENT IN EL SALVADOR RISES 60.5%

United States investment provided another encouraging economic headline.

According to figures reported by Diario El Mundo on October 4, US investment in El Salvador increased by 60.5%, reaching its highest reported investment position since late 2018.

Between April and June 2026, capital flows from the United States totaled approximately $144.41 million.

The development is especially relevant because the United States remains one of El Salvador's most important commercial and financial partners.

In a separate report published October 5, US authorities highlighted elements of El Salvador's investment framework, including dollarization, legal protections for investors and legislation supporting investment banking and alternative investment funds.

Together, these developments point to increasing interest in El Salvador's financial and business environment.

The reported capital flows and investment position are distinct measures, but both contribute to the broader picture of US economic engagement with El Salvador.

6. 🏗️ CHINA-DONATED NATIONAL STADIUM REACHES 75% COMPLETION

One of the country's most visible infrastructure projects continues moving toward completion.

The new national stadium, donated by the People's Republic of China, has reached approximately 75% construction progress.

Chinese Ambassador Zhang Yanhui reported that the stadium's seating was scheduled to arrive during the October 10–11 weekend, marking another stage in the development of the facility.

Designed to accommodate approximately 50,000 spectators, the stadium is intended to become a major venue for football, international sporting competitions and large-scale public events.

Beyond its seating capacity, the project represents a significant addition to El Salvador's sports and entertainment infrastructure.

When completed, the stadium could strengthen the country's ability to host events attracting regional and international visitors, supporting tourism, hospitality and related services.

The project also stands among the most recognizable examples of infrastructure cooperation between El Salvador and China.

7. ✈️ EL SALVADOR INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT SURPASSES FOUR MILLION PASSENGERS

El Salvador's principal international airport passed another important milestone this week.

By October 8, the airport had handled more than four million passengers in 2026, according to figures reported by Diario El Mundo.

The total includes passenger traffic associated with international travel, connections and transfers, reflecting the airport's role as both a Salvadoran gateway and a regional aviation hub.

Growing air connectivity is particularly important for tourism, international business, Salvadorans living abroad and commercial activity.

The milestone also reinforces the importance of continued airport modernization as passenger demand expands.

For El Salvador, an increasingly connected airport system is part of a wider effort to strengthen the country's position within Central American transportation and tourism networks.

8. 🛫 PACIFIC AIRPORT TERMINAL REACHES 30.14% CONSTRUCTION PROGRESS

Progress was also reported at the future Pacific Airport.

The construction of the airport's Beta terminal building reached 30.14%.

Work on the terminal's steel structure is expected to conclude in December 2026, while the first stage of the airport project is scheduled for mid-2027.

The Pacific Airport is intended to improve air connectivity in eastern El Salvador, a region with significant potential for tourism, commerce and investment.

Its development is particularly relevant to areas connected to the country's eastern coastline and the wider Surf City tourism strategy.

Although the project remains under construction, the reported progress offers a measurable update on one of El Salvador's major transportation investments.

9. 🇭🇳 MORE THAN 43,400 HONDURANS VISIT EL SALVADOR DURING SEMANA MORAZÁNICA

Thousands of Honduran visitors crossed into El Salvador during Semana Morazánica, the annual holiday period in Honduras.

By midday on October 8, Salvadoran migration authorities had recorded more than 43,400 entries by Honduran citizens, already exceeding the 43,008 recorded during the comparable 2025 holiday period.

The largest daily influx occurred on October 7, when more than 8,600 Honduran visitors entered the country.

Visitors traveled to enjoy beaches, restaurants, mountains, historic districts and other destinations.

Some were also drawn to the newly inaugurated Francisco Morazán mausoleum in San Salvador's historic center, connecting this week's tourism activity with last week's commemoration of the Central American leader.

The Salvadoran migration authority reported an expected total of approximately 48,300 entries for the holiday period, although one newspaper account cited a higher projection. The final result should be assessed against the official closing figure.

The influx is another example of the growing importance of regional tourism to El Salvador's hospitality and service industries.

10. 🏨 JW MARRIOTT SAN SALVADOR TAKES SHAPE AT MULTIPLAZA

El Salvador's luxury hospitality sector is preparing for another major addition.

The JW Marriott San Salvador project, located at Multiplaza, presented model rooms this week, offering an early look at the development's planned accommodations.

The project is designed to include 186 guest rooms and a theater, combining upscale hospitality with facilities that could support business travel, entertainment and events.

The investment reflects interest in higher-end accommodations as El Salvador attracts international travelers, business delegations and visitors seeking premium experiences.

The development also contributes to the broader transformation of the San Salvador metropolitan area's commercial and hospitality infrastructure.

For a country expanding its international tourism profile, new hotel capacity is an important component of long-term destination development.

11. 🏭 SALVADORAN INDUSTRY GROWS 3.6%

El Salvador's industrial sector recorded growth of 3.6%, according to figures highlighted by Diario El Salvador on October 6.

The sector accounts for approximately 12.7% of national gross domestic product, underscoring its importance to employment, production and the wider economy.

Industrial activity contributes to domestic supply chains while also supporting exports and the development of new commercial opportunities.

Its performance matters because a growing economy requires more than tourism and construction alone.

Manufacturing, industrial production, logistics and related services provide another foundation for economic diversification and formal employment.

The latest figures suggest that industry remains an important contributor to El Salvador's economic activity during 2026.

12. ₿ A NEW CHIVO SEEKS TO EXPAND FINANCIAL INCLUSION

El Salvador's Bitcoin and digital-finance sector also made headlines this week.

The new Chivo initiative presented plans to offer free remittances from the United States and expand access to credit for Salvadorans, including individuals without traditional banking relationships.

The proposal is significant because remittances remain an important source of household income for Salvadoran families.

Reducing transfer costs could allow recipients to retain more of the funds sent by relatives abroad.

Access to credit is another major element of the initiative, particularly for people who have historically faced barriers to conventional financial services.

The announcement outlines the new platform's ambitions; the practical impact will depend on its rollout, eligibility requirements and actual adoption.

Nevertheless, the project reflects continued efforts to connect digital financial services with everyday economic needs.

13. 🤖 LUIS RODRÍGUEZ PRESENTS NIX: AI FOR INVESTMENT AND ENVIRONMENTAL PLANNING

Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of El Salvador's institutional planning.

Luis Rodríguez, Executive Director of the San Salvador Metropolitan Area Planning Office (OPAMSS), presented NIX, an artificial-intelligence platform designed to support investment planning and environmental sustainability.

The presentation took place during the First Congress on Decentralized Cooperation in El Salvador.

According to @LRodriguez_SV, NIX is intended to improve strategic decision-making by providing territorial information relevant to investment and development across the San Salvador Metropolitan Area and the coastal region of La Libertad.

The initiative was developed with support from the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID), with Rodríguez also recognizing cooperation involving ESCO and the Embassy of Spain in El Salvador.

The significance of NIX extends beyond the introduction of another technology platform.

Urban development requires decisions involving land use, infrastructure, environmental conditions, economic opportunities and the long-term needs of growing communities.

AI-assisted planning tools could help public institutions and investors evaluate these factors more effectively.

For @COAMSS_OPAMSS, the initiative represents a new application of technology to territorial management and investment facilitation.

14. 🏘️ HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT REMAIN ON THE INTERNATIONAL AGENDA

El Salvador's housing and construction institutions continued participating in international cooperation and investment discussions.

Housing Minister @misol140, OPAMSS Executive Director Luis Rodríguez, representatives of the Salvadoran Chamber of Construction (@CASALCOsv) and business leaders participated in the Inter-American Development Bank's Housing Forum 2026.

The agenda included meetings and exchanges focused on housing development and opportunities for cooperation.

In another institutional activity, Tourism Minister @MorenaValdezSV joined Rodríguez, Adriana Larín of the Historic Center Authority (@AutoridadchSV), Paola Bardi of the DOT, business representatives and construction-sector technicians for a practical workshop.

These engagements highlight the relationship between housing, urban development, tourism and the investment climate.

As construction activity expands, coordination among public institutions, developers and international partners becomes increasingly relevant to the planning and execution of new projects.

THE BIGGER PICTURE: A COUNTRY BUILDING ACROSS MULTIPLE SECTORS

This week's headlines are notable not because they all concern one subject, but because they reflect developments across many parts of Salvadoran life.

A president leading an international approval ranking.

Two MS-13 members receiving life sentences.

A World Bank growth forecast raised to 4.5%.

Chevron announcing nearly $90 million in investment.

US investment figures showing renewed momentum.

A 50,000-seat stadium reaching 75% completion.

An international airport surpassing four million passengers.

Thousands of Hondurans crossing the border to spend their holidays in El Salvador.

New luxury accommodations, industrial growth, digital financial services and artificial-intelligence tools for urban planning.

Each story represents a different part of the country's economic, institutional and social landscape.

Taken together, they show a nation pursuing major projects while confronting the continuing challenges of economic development, public security and institutional modernization.

El Salvador's transformation is no longer a story confined to one headline. It is unfolding across airports, construction sites, courtrooms, businesses, tourist destinations and technology platforms.

And this week provided another opportunity to see that broader picture.

My father bought a house my mother had never seen, in a state they’d never visited or knew anyone (other than a distant cousin), and even then the infinite sacrifice of my parents was evident for my sister Claire (18 months younger than me) and I.

Even though my Dad initially worked pretty far away at the Ed Bluestein location (on South 183 not far from where the airport is now), he decided to buy a home in the Round Rock ISD, with the belief that the schools would be better than AISD by the time Claire and I needed them. It’s amazing how prescient that decision was, in retrospect.

Claire and I both attended National Blue Ribbon elementary (Laurel Mountain), middle (Canyon Vista) and high (Westwood) schools. You can read about how unlikely that is here (https://t.co/NdD2iWh1Gz) (TL:DR: It’s basically a 0.0034% chance in the U.S. to attend all three).

My childhood was idyllic. We were not wealthy, but we were comfortable. My father is the first person to attend and graduate from college in his family. His father worked three jobs to put him through Lehigh University (a baby Ivy known for their engineering school). My mother’s parents both attended and graduated from the University of Pittsburgh (#HailToPitt) and my mother graduated from Mount Union College in Alliance, OH. They both grew up in Pittsburgh (the cause of my intense #HereWeGo Steelers devotion), and went to rival high schools, meeting on a blind date and dating long distance throughout college in a very sweet love story.

After college, Dad immediately became an officer in the Coast Guard, so they got married on 12/26/70 as he had one day off from Coast Guard duties, and this year will celebrate their 56th (!!!) wedding anniversary.

My parents ran a tight ship.

How cool was I in high school?

My mother ran the sober prom committee. Need I say more?

But I played basketball all four years and worked for my excellent high school newspaper, where I began a lifelong love for journalism and benefitted from the mentorship, care and love of our journalism teacher, Judy Gaines.

My basketball season my senior year was akin to the film Hoosiers. Westwood had never won more than one playoff game in school history. That season, we improbably won four playoff games, decisively defeating two-time State Champion and undefeated #1 ranked Dallas Carter at the Ferrell Center in Waco. We ended up losing in the state semifinal to Midland Lee and my athletic career came to an end. I did have a consequential performance against Tomball in our first round playoff game, scoring 7 points in four minutes and erasing a 16 point deficit in the 3rd quarter. We won in overtime on a buzzer beater and our playoff run continued. I was carried off the court with people chanting my name, a truly bizarre, yet memorable experience.

I spent part of my spring visiting colleges with my father. My top list of schools was: Notre Dame, Northwestern, Washington & Lee, and Rhodes College. I was rejected by all. My fallbacks (arrogant term, I know) were: Lehigh University (my Dad’s alma mater), UT and Texas A&M. I got into all three.

I might have been able to walk on to the Lehigh basketball team, but was afraid of the brutal winters, isolated campus, and uphill walk everyday (literally). Texas A&M didn’t seem a fit for me.

So I reluctantly accepted UT, mildly depressed that I was not ‘going away for school’.

Almost overnight, I began having what would become an extraordinary experience in my five (victory lap!) years at UT. I joined a mid-size blue collar fraternity (Delta Chi), served as pledge class president, rush chair, social chair, and President for two years. I was Interfraternity Council (IFC) President. I was accepted into UT’s most elite men’s service and leadership organization, Texas Cowboys. I ran two successful Student Body President campaigns. And I was appointed to the President’s Student Advisory Committee (PSAC), and got to know and remain friends with the legendary former UT President Dr. Larry Faulker (we both attend Covenant Presbyterian with our brides).

I don’t mention these things to relive former glories. I mention them to explain why I am eternally indebted to Austin, and to my parents for their love and sacrifice.

I graduated UT debt-free (a true blessing) after a semester working at the Texas Legislature (adjacent) for a well known state lobbyist, Julie Moore, who worked for Oxy and whose father was an absolute legend who founded the Austin Club. She has been one of my most important mentors in my life, even to this day.

I spent my last Spring Break beating the pavement in DC, and the day after I graduated from UT in May 2003 I moved to Washington, DC with no job. I was able to live with a family member (my mother’s sister Mary Lou McGee and her husband Bob McGee in their beautiful suburban Maryland home). They could not have been more welcoming or lovely. Uncle Bob also became a special and impactful mentor to me.

Six weeks later, I earned an interim security clearance and began working for the #3 official at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, not two years removed from 9/11. It was a heady place to work in your first job out of high school, surrounded by deeply serious people who spent every waking minute protecting Americans. It was the honor of a lifetime to work amongst them in my own small way.

My time in DC (8 years) included working as a Press Secretary for two U.S. Senators, working in White House advance (Presidential and Vice Presidential), and running the second largest county in Iowa on Bush-Cheney re-election campaign in 2004 (a state we won for the first time in 20 years). In June 2009, I left U.S. Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison’s office after two formative, grueling, and incredible years, and launched my consulting firm, Potomac Strategy Group, with the hope of building a business and returning to Texas, hopefully to marry a Texas girl and settle down.

I could keep going. But I won’t in service to you if you’ve read this far already.

The point of this personal story is this: I have infinite gratitude to Austin, for forming me, and to my parents, Larry & Georgia Mackowiak, for instilling in me the critical values of hard work, integrity, honesty, and service to others, all honoring our Christian faith (I was raised Catholic). Whatever I am, it is probably equal parts nature (Austin) and nurture (my family).

This brings me to @SaveAustinNow.

I returned to Austin in late 2011, initially living at Brazos Place downtown and opening an office across the street in the legendary Vaughn Building (where I still office today).

Early on, I did not concern myself with local matters. Mayor Lee Leffingwell appeared to be a serious person and the city was reasonably well led.

Only when the worst Mayor in the history of Austin (Steve Adler) allowed Comrade Greg Casar to engineer and pass the Homeless Camping Ordinance (an idea that has never succeeded anywhere it’s been tried), did I begin to take notice and decide something must be done.

The rest of the story is probably well known.

It took my Democratic co-founder (Cleo Petricek, to whom I remain truly grateful) and I TWO YEARS and TWO PETITION DRIVES to put on the ballot and pass Prop B (reinstatement of the Camping Ban), which we did over the objection of 9/10 council members and Mayor Adler, as well as nearly every Democratic official in Travis County. Our 58-42% victory, with more than 90,000 votes in our favor, saved Austin. We would be Portland had we failed. This is not hyperbole.

What began in 2019 has now become the largest grassroots organization in Austin history and it’s not even close.

We have:
> 232,000 email subscribers
> 90,000 email opens in 6-8 hours
> $7M+ raised in nearly 8 years from 7,000+ individual donors
> Massive social media and earned media presence
> Thousands of volunteers

But what have we accomplished?

We have won two major elections (Prop B and last year’s defeat of Prop Q, the morally bankrupt and idiotic 20% city property tax increase), and after losing Prop A (to overturn defund the police) passed the same policy with the state legislature (with Democratic votes in both Houses).

After ten months of work, we are now 25 days from passing the most sweeping structural reform in Austin history — the Outside Audit Charter Amendment (https://t.co/OuGC0W2dea), which is both common sense and making all the right people mad (as I wrote about yesterday, here -- https://t.co/3e8Lq0QSHt).

And we are just getting started.

I’ll finish with this.

We CANNOT do what we do, with the focus and intensity it requires, without your support and encouragement.

It takes resources to build and run an organization like this. Every one of my six employees works on Save Austin Now, and one employee spends 95% of his time on it. I probably spend 2/3 of my time on it, while running a business with six employees (https://t.co/XQXFK0fdH1), serving for 3+ years as CEO of the Austin Baseball Commission (https://t.co/07Li3FEVXS) which will bring a MLB team to Austin, serving my private clients, opening a bar on 6th street (which I co-own, https://t.co/Z50ueTsLpp) and being a husband to the ever patient and lovely Amy and father to our 10 month old son Jack and our two aodrable rescue dogs, Princess Hope and Prince Harry.

Saving Austin is something we all care about deeply.

But Save Austin Now is JUST BUILT DIFFERENT.

We will not let Austin become Portland. We will not allow our police to be defunded and unsupported. We will not allow open homeless camping. We will not allow the continued mistreatment of taxpayers.

Our commitment is total.

Thank you for all this support through the years.

We really do need more support to accomplish our goals in 25 days. I am not just saying that.

If you believe in me, and in us, and in our mission, and that Austin must be — and can be — saved, please consider supporting us right here right now — https://t.co/JtIpiHfqyJ. You can also Venmo to @saveaustinnow or make a check to “Save Austin Now” and mail it to 807 Brazos St., Ste. 306, Austin, TX 78701.

Again, thank you from the bottom of my heart.

THE LIE OF 'RENEWABLE' ENERGY
Oct 9, 2026 · Jonathan Cohler

They are not 'renewable.' The materials run out fast. The supply chains run on child labor and forced labor. The equipment runs on fossil fuels. The whole system is a one-generation extraction cycle with a green label slapped on top. Calling it 'renewable' is a lie.

Nothing about this is 'renewable.'

Nothing about this is 'clean.'

Nothing about this is 'ethical.'

Calling it any of these things is a lie.

INTRODUCTION
Say the word 'renewable' and a normal person hears 'this does not run out.' That is the lie.

The sunlight does not run out. The wind does not run out. The machines that catch them are made of metals, and the choke-point metals run out fast. Dysprosium, within this generation. Silver, meaningfully drawn down across several build cycles. Tellurium, already at a hard cap for the thin-film technology that uses it. Neodymium and lithium reserves are not immediately exhausted, but the Chinese separation and conversion chokepoints already bind the chain.

A big wind turbine needs a magnet. That magnet needs a metal called dysprosium. The world mines about 2,000 tons of dysprosium a year, roughly 87 percent from China and 11 percent from Myanmar. The separation step that turns ore into usable metal is almost entirely Chinese, and that choke point already governs global allocation. Studies put cumulative demand through 2050 at 176,000 to 318,000 tons, which crosses China's current stated dysprosium reserve somewhere between 2032 and 2049. Global reserves outside Myanmar sit around 800,000 tons in that literature; the whole stock is not drained, but the Chinese slice is. A separate China-demand study puts electric vehicle motors at 41 to 56 percent of cumulative dysprosium demand through 2050 and wind at 18 to 24 percent. EVs are the bigger pull.

A solar panel needs silver. One big push to replace power plants with solar uses up roughly a fifth of the known silver reserves. The panels wear out in 25 years and have to be built again. Thrifting and recycling stretch the supply. At the stated buildout the silver draw is still a serious fraction of global reserves across several decades of maintenance.

One kind of thin solar panel uses a metal called tellurium. The world only produces enough tellurium each year to make a tiny slice of the solar panels being built. That kind of panel cannot scale. Full stop.

A share of Congo's cobalt is dug out by hand in artisanal pits. The artisanal fraction of Congolese supply has fallen from about 20 percent in the mid-2010s to a few percent today, but it is where the child labor sits. UNICEF estimated in 2014 that about 40,000 children worked in all mines across southern Congo. A 2024 Congolese government report identified 16,845 children specifically in the cobalt chain between 2019 and 2022, most between 12 and 17. People die in collapsed pits. Amnesty International, the BBC, the Washington Post, and NBC have all documented it.

China produced about 93 percent of the world's polysilicon in 2024. Xinjiang's share of world polysilicon output has run from the mid-20s to about 45 percent depending on year. Forced labor of Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang's polysilicon production is documented by the US government, the UK government, Sheffield Hallam University, and the Associated Press, and triggers US import restrictions under the UFLPA.

When the turbines wear out in 20 years, the blades mostly get buried in US landfills. Europe runs them through cement kilns, where the glass becomes raw material and the resin burns as kiln fuel. The panels get crushed; most go to landfill because recycling costs more than the recovered material is worth. The batteries get thrown out at low recycling rates.

The sunlight is free. The wind is free. The machinery is a strip mine with a 20-year expiration date, drawing on a cobalt supply chain with a small but documented artisanal fraction worked in part by children, shipped on diesel freighters, and dumped in a hole.

The numbers behind the TRUTH
For anyone who wants to check the math. Mining and reserve figures from USGS, buildout figures from IEA, dysprosium demand scenarios from the published 2022-to-2050 cumulative-demand paper and a separate China-demand study, cobalt supply breakdown from the Cobalt Institute, labor figures from UNICEF, Amnesty International, and the Congolese government's 2024 cobalt-chain report, polysilicon figures from Bernreuter Research and Sheffield Hallam University, forced-labor findings from the US (UFLPA) and UK government.

THE METALS
Neodymium. World rare earth oxide mine output was about 390,000 tons in 2024. Praseodymium-neodymium oxide supply was roughly 90,000 tons, approximately balanced with magnet demand. Nd oxide prices fell from about $134/kg in 2022 to about $56/kg in 2024. The constraint shows up at scale and by turbine type: direct-drive permanent-magnet turbines use roughly 180 kg Nd/MW; geared turbines use 12 to 50 kg/MW. Most onshore wind is geared. The pressure point is scaled offshore direct-drive, plus EV motors (the larger growth term), plus electronics, plus defense, all drawing on the same stream. Refining and separation of neodymium is almost entirely controlled by China.

Dysprosium. Production is roughly 1,000 to 2,000 tons a year. Over 1988 to 2021 the mine split was about 87 percent China and 11 percent Myanmar; separation is near-total Chinese control. Dy is a small fraction of rare earth deposits and the heavy rare earth that gives NdFeB magnets their high-temperature performance for offshore service. The 2022-to-2050 cumulative demand range of 176,000 to 318,000 tons crosses China's current stated dysprosium reserve in 2032, 2034, 2038, or 2040 under the static case, moving to 2038 to 2049 if that reserve grows at 2 percent a year. USGS does not publish a dysprosium reserve; the Chinese figure comes from the referenced literature. Global reserves outside Myanmar sit around 800,000 tons in that same literature; the cumulative range does not drain that stock, but it does drain the Chinese share. A separate study of China's own dysprosium demand puts electric vehicles at 41 to 56 percent of cumulative demand and wind at 18 to 24 percent. Dy-reduced and Dy-free magnet research exists; it is not yet the volume product.

Terbium. About 400 tons a year of production. Loadings in magnets are a fraction of Dy loadings. Not a one-buildout exhaustion story, but another concentrated supply with no non-Chinese refining at scale.

What binds first. Dysprosium at scaled EV motor and permanent-magnet wind production is the first heavy rare earth to bind hard. Cumulative demand to 2050 crosses China's current stated dysprosium reserve in the 2032-to-2040 window under the static-reserve case, moving to 2038-to-2049 if that reserve grows at 2 percent a year, if magnet chemistries stay Dy-rich. Global reserves outside Myanmar (~800,000 tons) are not drained by that cumulative range, but the China-concentrated share is. Terbium is a concentrated supply with no non-Chinese refining at scale; lower loadings than dysprosium mean a longer exhaustion timeline, and the geopolitical dependency is identical. Neodymium reserves are not immediately exhausted, but the Chinese refining chokepoint can close overnight, and reserves held in uneconomic grades do not substitute for refined metal on any useful timescale.

SOLAR
Silver. Crystalline silicon cells use about 10 tons of silver per gigawatt, down from about 50 tons/GW roughly fifteen years ago through aggressive thrifting. World silver mine production was 25,300 tons in 2024. USGS reserves are 610,000 tons. Photovoltaics took roughly 6,000 tons in 2024, around a quarter of mine output. A 12,400 GW scaled buildout at 10 tons/GW requires about 124,000 tons of silver, roughly a fifth of known reserves. One buildout. Then rebuild every 25 years. Compounded against industrial, electronics, and jewelry demand, the pressure is real; the reserves are not immediately exhausted.

Tellurium. Cadmium telluride thin film is roughly 5 percent of the module market. Modern CdTe cells use about 15 tons Te/GW. World refinery output is around 1,000 tons a year, already a hard cap on how much CdTe can be built annually. CdTe cannot scale to carry the whole market.

Indium. Byproduct of zinc refining with roughly 900 tons a year of output. A constraint on CIGS thin film and on transparent conductors, not on the dominant silicon PV path.

Polysilicon. Not a scarcity problem. An energy problem (silicon purification is coal-fired in Xinjiang) and a labor problem (documented forced labor in that same region). Covered below.

Copper, Aluminum, and the Grid
The IEA figure of about 80 million kilometers of new transmission and distribution by 2040 is real. High-voltage overhead transmission conductors are predominantly aluminum (ACSR, AAC, AAAC). Copper dominates in distribution cabling, generator windings, EV motors, and building wiring. USGS copper reserves are about 980 million tons; mine production was about 23 million tons a year in 2024 and 2025.

Ore grades have fallen over the last century. Industry shorthand puts the drop from about 2 percent copper in 1900 to about 0.5 percent today; this is a sector-wide approximation, not a USGS global time series, and the decline is real but uneven across deposits. Lower grade means more rock, more diesel, more water, and more energy per ton. The scaling cost of continued extraction is where the system actually binds, not a single reserve-exhaustion number.

STORAGE
The wind does not blow all the time. The sun sets every night. Any intermittent-generation system needs firming.

Lithium mine production reached about 222,000 tons in 2024 and an estimated 290,000 tons in 2025. USGS reserves are around 37 million tons. The resource is not immediately scarce. The pressure is on refining, cell manufacturing, and the pace of capacity growth.

Backing one day of US electricity (about 11 TWh) entirely with lithium-ion batteries is impractical. That is a design choice. Pumped hydro, long-duration flow batteries, compressed air, hydrogen, and massive overbuild with curtailment are the alternatives. Each carries its own materials bill and its own siting problem. A grid-scale firming solution matched to a wind-and-solar-dominant system at full load, through winter and dark weeks, at any defensible cost, does not exist today.

THE CHILDREN
More than 70 percent of the world's cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The artisanal share of Congolese production has fallen from about 20 percent in the mid-2010s to a few percent today, but it is where the child labor sits. Children work in unregulated pits with no safety gear and die in collapsed workings for a few dollars a day.

UNICEF's 2014 estimate counted about 40,000 children working in all mines across southern Congo, not cobalt alone. A 2024 Congolese government report identified 16,845 children specifically in the cobalt chain from 2019 to 2022, most between the ages of 12 and 17. Amnesty International, the Washington Post, Sky News, the BBC, and NBC have documented the artisanal cobalt labor conditions. Siddharth Kara's 2023 book Cobalt Red lays out the artisanal system in detail.

The cobalt goes to trading houses, then to Chinese refineries, then into the batteries that power electric cars and store wind and solar electricity. Industrial Congolese cobalt and artisanal cobalt enter the same refining chain. Chain-of-custody auditing has improved but cannot fully segregate the artisanal fraction once it enters the mixed smelter stream.

China produced about 93 percent of the world's polysilicon in 2024. Xinjiang's share of world polysilicon output has run from the mid-20s to about 45 percent depending on year. Documented forced labor of Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang's polysilicon production has been confirmed by the US government (UFLPA), the UK government, Sheffield Hallam University, and the Associated Press. Panels built with Xinjiang polysilicon are blocked at US borders unless importers can prove otherwise.

Lithium in the Atacama Desert is drawn as brine at rates documented to lower water tables and depress freshwater availability for indigenous Atacameño communities who have farmed that land for a thousand years. The water conflict is real and the communities are losing ground. The lithium goes to batteries.

Nickel in Indonesia and the Philippines is clearing rainforest and running rivers red with laterite tailings. Workers die in refineries that would not pass a safety inspection anywhere in the West.

Rare earth mining in Baotou, Inner Mongolia has produced a radioactive sludge lake miles across. Farmers downwind report elevated cancer rates. Livestock die. Crops fail. Baotou (the Bayan Obo deposit) is the main source of light rare earths including neodymium. The heavy rare earths that permanent-magnet offshore wind depends on, dysprosium and terbium, come from southern Chinese ionic clay deposits and from Myanmar, with their own documented environmental harms.

The industry is built on this. Not as an unfortunate side effect. As a structural dependency. Separated dysprosium and terbium at volume have no non-Chinese substitute at current prices and current refining capacity; Lynas has begun separated heavy-REE output but at tons per quarter, not at scale. Polysilicon has non-Xinjiang alternatives, both non-Xinjiang Chinese capacity and non-Chinese capacity (Wacker and others), and the market is adjusting under US import restrictions, though Xinjiang still carries a large share. Cobalt has partial alternatives (Indonesia supplied about 14 percent of mined cobalt in 2025), but the artisanal Congolese stream still enters the same mixed refining chain.

THE WASTE
Solar panels last 25 years. Wind turbine blades last 20 years. Lithium batteries last 10 to 15 years.

Wind blades are fiberglass and epoxy and cannot be melted down. US practice is landfill: blades are cut with diamond saws and buried in enormous landfills in Wyoming, Iowa, Texas, and elsewhere. Europe has moved to commercial cement-kiln co-processing, where the glass becomes raw material and the resin burns as kiln fuel. China's Solid Waste Law bans landfilling blade composites; the modeled routes are incineration, cement-kiln co-processing, pyrolysis, and mechanical recycling, but recycling capacity is still underdeveloped and not industrialized.

Supplemental Coverage vs. Proprietary Hardware
• Starlink’s Approach: Uses existing terrestrial operator spectrum. To avoid interfering with adjacent ground networks, Starlink’s Direct-to-Cell must operate under strict power flux density (PFD) limits mandated by the FCC and ITU.
• The AST Advantage: AST SpaceMobile was built ground-up with massive phased-array apertures. These giant antennas achieve vastly superior link budgets without violating PFD limits, allowing high-bandwidth 5G voice, data, and video directly to standard smartphones.

2. Service Quality: Text messaging vs. True 5G Broadband

• Starlink Direct-to-Cell primarily targets basic text, messaging, emergency alerts, and low-bandwidth telemetry due to array size constraints on standard satellite buses.
• AST targets full broadband throughput (data rates capable of video streaming, full internet access, and voice calls) without specialized satellite hardware inside the phone.

3. T-Mobile and Multi-Operator Realities

• Mobile Network Operators rarely rely on single-source vendor exclusivity for critical coverage.
• AST already holds partnerships and commercial agreements with major global telcos (including AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, and Google). A potential $TMUS or broader operator expansion toward AST remains viable because operators need real 5G broadband speeds, not just SMS backup, to monetize premium direct-to-device add-on tiers.

Government & Defense Demand
